'''Brighton Beach''',{{efn|{{Langx|ru|Брайтон-Бич}}}} also referred to as '''Little Odessa''',{{efn|{{Langx|ru|Маленькая Одесса|Malenkaya Odessa}}}} or '''Little Russia''',{{efn|{{langx|ru|Маленькая Россия|Malenkaya Rossiya}}}}<ref>{{cite news |title=A little corner of Russia in New York |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/10581932 |work=BBC News |date=9 July 2010 |archive-date=December 4, 2011 |access-date=August 22, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111204035224/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/10581932 |url-status=live }}</ref> is a [[List of Brooklyn neighborhoods|neighborhood]] in the southern portion of the [[New York City]] [[Borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Brooklyn]], within the greater [[Coney Island]] area along the [[Atlantic Ocean]] coastline.<ref name=":0" /> Brighton Beach is bounded by Coney Island proper at [[Ocean Parkway (Brooklyn)|Ocean Parkway]] to the west, [[Manhattan Beach, Brooklyn|Manhattan Beach]] at Corbin Place to the east, [[Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn|Sheepshead Bay]] at the [[Belt Parkway]] to the north, and the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the south along the beach and [[Riegelmann Boardwalk|boardwalk]].

It is known for its high population of [[Russian Americans in New York City|Russian-speaking immigrants]], and as a summer destination for New York City residents due to its beaches along the Atlantic Ocean and its proximity to the amusement parks in Coney Island. It was named in the 1870s as an allusion to the English resort city of [[Brighton]].

Brighton Beach is part of [[Brooklyn Community Board 13|Brooklyn Community District 13]], and its primary [[ZIP Code]] is 11235.<ref name="NYCPlanning" /> It is patrolled by the 60th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department]].<ref name="NYPD 60th Precinct" /> Politically, Brighton Beach is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 48th District.<ref name=":1">[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/brooklyn.pdf Current City Council Districts for Kings County] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170131103455/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/brooklyn.pdf |date=January 31, 2017 }}, [[New York City]]. Retrieved May 5, 2017.</ref>

== History ==
=== Early development ===
{{stack|float=left|

Brighton Beach is included in an area from Sheepshead Bay to Sea Gate that was purchased from the Native Americans in 1645 for a gun, a blanket and a kettle.<ref name="Douglass">{{cite journal|last=Douglass|first=Harvey |year = 1933| title=Coney Island Scenes Shift, Never Change | url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/59998009/ |journal=The Brooklyn Daily Eagle |access-date=March 23, 2016}}</ref>

Brighton Beach was located on sandy terrain, and before development in the 1860s, had mostly farms. The area was part of the "Middle Division" of the town of [[Gravesend, Brooklyn|Gravesend]], which was the sole English settlement out of the original six towns in [[Brooklyn|Kings County]]. By the mid-18th century, thirty-nine lots in the division had been distributed to the descendants of English colonists.<ref name="Williams" />

In 1868, [[William A. Engeman]] built a resort in the area.<ref name="Coney Island Hotels" /> The resort was given the name "Brighton Beach" in 1878 by [[Henry C. Murphy]] and a group of businessmen, who chose the name as an allusion to the English resort city of [[Brighton]].<ref name="Citycyclopedia">{{cite book |author=Weinstein, Stephen |editor1=Jackson, Kenneth T. |editor2=Keller, Lisa |editor3=Flood, Nancy |editor-link= Kenneth T. Adjacent to the hotel, Engeman built the [[Brighton Beach Race Course]] for [[thoroughbred]] [[horse racing]].<ref name="Coney Island Hotels" /> In December 1887, an extremely high tide washed over the area, creating a new, temporary connection between Sheepshead Bay and the ocean. Wrote the ''[[Brooklyn Daily Eagle]]'': "Unless [Engeman] is very lucky the next races on the Brighton Beach track will be conducted by the white crested horses of [[Neptune (mythology)|Neptune]]."<ref>{{cite news |date=December 10, 1887 |title=High Tides |url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50379357/ |access-date=July 29, 2012 |newspaper=Brooklyn Daily Eagle |archive-date=December 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181215070012/https://bklyn.newspapers.com/image/50379357/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

After that extremely high tide, and a decade of [[Coastal erosion|beach erosion]], the Brighton Beach Hotel, by then owned by the Railway, faced the possibility of being "undermined and carried away."<ref name="SciAmer1888">{{cite journal|title=Moving the Brighton Beach Hotel|journal=Scientific American|location=New York|date=April 14, 1888|quote=Reprinted as "A Hotel on Wheels," in ''The Engineer'' (London, ENG), April 27, 1888|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/magazine/sa/1888/04-14/|access-date=November 12, 2015|archive-date=November 12, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151112201358/http://www.scientificamerican.com/magazine/sa/1888/04-14/|url-status=live}}{{subscription required|date=November 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://arrts-arrchives.com/brbchmove.html |title=Brighton Beach |publisher=Arrts-arrchives.com |date=May 11, 2004 |access-date=November 12, 2015 |archive-date=January 19, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160119095459/http://arrts-arrchives.com/brbchmove.html |url-status=live }}</ref> A "highly ingenious and novel" plan to elevate and move the entire building was begun by railway Superintendent J.L. Morrow and Secretary E.L. Langford. It was accomplished by lifting the entire estimated 5000-ton {{convert|460|x|150|ft|m}} hotel on 13 hydraulic jacks, raising the building above its plot, and then laying 24 lines of railroad track – a mile and a half long altogether – under it; then the building temporarily on 112 railroad "platform cars" (flat cars) was pulled by six steam [[locomotive]]s and relocated another 495 feet inland.<ref name="SciAmer1888" /> This careful engineering (by B.C. Miller) made the move successful; it began on April 2, 1888, and continued for nine days, and was the largest building relocation of the 19th century.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Big Hotel on Wheels|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=April 4, 1888|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1888/04/14/archives/the-big-hotel-on-wheels.html|access-date=November 12, 2015|archive-date=July 28, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180728003039/https://www.nytimes.com/1888/04/14/archives/the-big-hotel-on-wheels.html|url-status=live}}{{subscription required|date=November 2015}}</ref>

[[Anton Seidl]] and the [[Metropolitan Opera]] brought their popular interpretations of [[Richard Wagner|Wagner]] to the Brighton Beach Music Hall, where [[John Philip Sousa]] was in residence, and the New Brighton Theater was a hotspot for vaudeville. Visitors for tea at [[Reisenweber's Brighton Beach Casino]] would be served by Japanese waitresses in full costume. At an enormous private club, the Brighton Beach Baths, members could swim, access a private beach, and play [[American handball|handball]], [[mah-jongg]], and cards.<ref name="Williams" />

The village, along with the rest of Gravesend, was annexed into the 31st Ward of the [[City of Brooklyn]] in 1894.<ref>{{cite book | title=Appleton's Dictionary of New York and Vicinity | year=1904 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MzUWAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA66 | access-date=November 12, 2015 | page=66}}</ref>

=== Early 20th century ===
In 1905, Brighton Beach Park opened its own area of amusements, called Brighton Pike. Brighton Pike offered a boardwalk, games, live entertainment (including the [[Miller Brothers 101 Ranch|Miller Brothers]]' wild-west show: ''[[101 Ranch Wild West Show|101 Ranch]]''), and a huge steel roller coaster. In May 1919, most of the park was burned down, including the roller coaster.<ref name="Williams" /><ref name=":1" /> The beach remained popular.<ref name="Our Brooklyn 1936" />

Brighton Beach was re-developed as a fairly dense residential community with the final rebuilding of the Brighton Beach railway to [[rapid transit]] standards, becoming the [[Brooklyn–Manhattan Transit Corporation]] (BMT)'s Brighton Line, which opened as a subway line in August 1920 (the line is now served by the [[New York City Subway]]'s {{NYCS trains|Brighton|type=service}}). The subway line within the neighborhood is above ground on an elevated structure. The opening of the BMT Brighton Line had conflicting consequences: although it made Brighton Beach viable as a year-round community, it was now much more feasible for visitors to return home in the evening rather than spend the night. This led to the closure of the Brighton Beach Hotel in 1924.<ref name="Williams" />

The years just before and following the [[Great Depression]] brought with them a neighborhood consisting mostly of first- and second-generation Jewish-Americans and, later, [[Holocaust]] [[concentration camp]] survivors.<ref name="Internet Archive 2008" /><ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hatX-W6PCEEC |title=New Immigrants in New York |author=Nancy Foner |isbn=978-0-231-12415-7 |publisher=Columbia University Press |date=2001 |access-date=November 12, 2015}}</ref> Of the estimated 55,000 Holocaust survivors living in New York City as of 2011, most live in Brighton Beach.<ref>{{cite news |author=Suddath, Claire |year=2010 |work=Time (online, November 13) |title=The Plot to Cheat Germany's Holocaust Survivors' Fund |url=http://www.time.com/time/nation/article/0,8599,2031278,00.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101116121852/http://www.time.com/time/nation/article/0,8599,2031278,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 16, 2010 | access-date=November 11, 2015}}</ref> To meet the bursting cultural demands, the New Brighton Theater converted itself to the States' first Yiddish theater in 1919.<ref name="Williams" /><ref name="Internet Archive 2008">{{cite web|title=Coney Island and the Jews|website=Internet Archive|date=November 27, 2008|url=https://archive.org/details/coneyislandjews00york|access-date=November 13, 2015}}</ref>

=== Late 20th century and Soviet immigration ===
[[File:Театр Миллениум.jpg|thumb|right|The "Millennium Theater", now the "Master Theater" and NetCost supermarket]]

After [[World War II]], the quality of life in Brighton Beach decreased significantly as the poverty rate and the ratio of older residents to younger residents increased; this was primarily effectuated by the postwar codification of [[rent regulation in New York]], which incentivized middle-aged residents and retirees (particularly the aforementioned first- and second-generation Jewish-American residents, many of whom had eschewed homeownership in favor of investing their savings in family businesses or postsecondary educations for their children) to retain their units in the prewar six-story semi-fireproof elevator apartment houses that lined Brightwater Court and other nearby thoroughfares for decades.<ref name="Our Brooklyn 1936" /> During the [[History of New York City (1946–77)|1970s fiscal crisis]], the exodus of government workers and other middle class residents to suburban areas accelerated; accordingly, many of Brighton Beach's freestanding houses and bungalows were subdivided into [[single room occupancy]] residences for the poor, the elderly and the mentally ill. Brighton Beach suffered from arson as much as it did from constant drug trades.<ref name="Our Brooklyn 1936" /> During the summer, however, people from all around the city continued to flock to Brighton Beach's beach next to the Atlantic Ocean.<ref name="Our Brooklyn 1936" />

In the mid-1970s, Brighton Beach became a popular place to settle for [[Russian Americans in New York City|Soviet immigrants]], mostly [[Ashkenazi Jews]] from [[Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|Russia]] and [[Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic|Ukraine]].<ref name="Our Brooklyn 1936" /> So many Soviet Jews immigrated to Brighton Beach that the area became known as "Little [[Odessa]]" (after the Ukrainian city on the [[Black Sea]] with a significant Jewish population in the first half of 20th century).<ref name="Our Brooklyn 1936" />

The 1991 [[collapse of the Soviet Union]] and the subsequent significant changes in the social and economic circumstances of post-Soviet states led thousands of former Soviet citizens to immigrate to the United States.<ref name="Our Brooklyn 1936" /> Many more immigrants from the former Soviet Union, who primarily spoke [[Russian language|Russian]], chose Brighton Beach as a place to settle.<ref>[https://hesterstreet.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Brighton-Beach_Final-Report.pdf#page=3 ''Brighton Beach: Strengthening Community Resiliency – Final Report''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240420130331/https://hesterstreet.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Brighton-Beach_Final-Report.pdf#page=3 |date=April 20, 2024 }}, Hester Street, February 2016. Retrieved August 16, 2024. "Brighton Beach, located on one of the nation's most iconic urban beach fronts, has long been a neighborhood of immigrants. Following the fall of the Soviet Union, a wave of Russian immigrants settled in Brighton Beach."</ref> This included an influx of immigrants from the [[Caucasus]], mostly from countries such as [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] and [[Azerbaijan]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/14/nyregion/brighton-beach-photo-essay.html|title=Welcome to Брайтон Бич, Brooklyn|last1=Yurenev|first1=Alexey|date=December 14, 2018|work=The New York Times|access-date=January 26, 2020|last2=Akhtiorskaya|first2=Yelena|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=January 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190104021736/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/14/nyregion/brighton-beach-photo-essay.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://globalcitynyc.com/|title=Global City NYC|website=Global City NYC|access-date=January 26, 2020|archive-date=January 26, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200126040722/http://globalcitynyc.com/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://immigrationtounitedstates.org/507-former-soviet-union-immigrants.html|title=Former Soviet Union immigrants|website=Immigration to the United States|language=en|access-date=January 26, 2020|archive-date=January 26, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200126040645/https://immigrationtounitedstates.org/507-former-soviet-union-immigrants.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

A large number of Russian immigrant firms, shops, restaurants, clubs, offices, banks, schools, and children's play centers opened in the area.<ref name="jewish daily forward 201209" /> The value of real estate in Brighton Beach started to rise again, even though drugs remained a social issue in the area through the early 1990s.<ref name="Our Brooklyn 1936" />

In the early 2000s, a high-income ocean-front condominium complex, the "Oceana", was constructed.<ref>{{cite news|author=Sheftell, Jason|year=2008|title=Oceana – a residential resort village off Brighton Beach's main drag|newspaper=Daily News|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/life-style/real-estate/oceana-residential-resort-village-brighton-beach-main-drag-article-1.316028|access-date=November 12, 2015|archive-date=November 12, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151112201358/http://www.nydailynews.com/life-style/real-estate/oceana-residential-resort-village-brighton-beach-main-drag-article-1.316028|url-status=live}}</ref> This address has become the destination of wealthy businessmen, entertainers, and senior officials from the former Soviet Union, and with their purchase of units at the Oceana, area housing prices have risen.<ref name="jewish daily forward 201209">{{cite web|author1=Larson, Michael|author2=Liao, Bingling|author3=Stulberg, Ariel|author4=Kordunsky, Anna|year=2012|title=Changing Face of Brighton Beach: Central Asians Join Russian Jews in Brooklyn Neighborhood.|publisher=[[The Jewish Daily Forward]]|url=http://forward.com/articles/162963/changing-face-of-brighton-beach/|access-date=November 11, 2015|archive-date=February 15, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150215222312/http://forward.com/articles/162963/changing-face-of-brighton-beach/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Since the early 2010s, a significant number of [[Central Asia]]n immigrants have also chosen Brighton Beach as a place to settle.<ref name="jewish daily forward 201209" />

Today, Brighton Beach has many synagogues and Jewish institutions, including a [[Chabad]] center,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chabadneshama.com/templates/articlecco_cdo/aid/89655/jewish/About-us.htm|title=About us – Chabad Neshama Center|access-date=February 18, 2022|archive-date=February 19, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220219160913/https://www.chabadneshama.com/templates/articlecco_cdo/aid/89655/jewish/About-us.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> a [[Mikvah]] and a Jewish day school called Mazel.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mazeldayschool.com/templates/articlecco_cdo/aid/2956935/jewish/Our-History.htm|title=Our History – Mazel Day School – Independent Jewish Preschool and K-8 School|access-date=February 18, 2022|archive-date=February 19, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220219183937/https://www.mazeldayschool.com/templates/articlecco_cdo/aid/2956935/jewish/Our-History.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Russian-speaking culture ===
[[File:Storefront of NY Central Pharmacy.jpg|thumb|A Brighton Beach storefront's sign, which features both its English and Russian names.]]
As apartment buildings started to be built in large numbers in the 1930s, many of those who moved into the neighborhood were Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe, often by way of the Lower East Side. They came from many countries, but also set the stage for a later wave of [[History of the Jews in the United States|Jewish immigration]] from the Soviet Union that started in the 1970s, when Brighton Beach became known as "Little Odessa,"<ref name="nickname">{{cite web |url=http://untappedcities.com/2014/01/23/nyc-micro-neighborhoods-little-odessa-brighton-beach-brooklyn/ |title=NYC's Micro Neighborhoods: Little Odessa in Brighton Beach, Brooklyn |year=2014 |work=Untapped Cities (online, January 23) |author=Ortiz, Brennan |access-date=September 9, 2014 |archive-date=October 31, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031195856/https://untappedcities.com/2014/01/23/nyc-micro-neighborhoods-little-odessa-brighton-beach-brooklyn/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="NYC Parks Boardwalk" /> and "Little Russia".<ref>{{cite book |author=Johnstone, Sarah |title=Ukraine |publisher=Lonely Planet |location=Melbourne, AUS |date=2005 |page=119}}</ref> An annual festival, the Brighton Jubilee, celebrates the area's [[Russian language in the United States|Russian-speaking heritage]], being populated heavily by [[Russian Americans in New York City|Russian]], [[Belarusian Americans in New York City|Belarusian Americans]], and [[Ukrainian Americans in New York City|Ukrainian Americans]].<ref name="Williams" /> The area has also been called "the land of [[pelmeni]], [[matryoshka]]s, [[tracksuit]]s, and...[[vodka]]" due to its large population of Soviet immigrants.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Idov, Michael |year=2009 |title=New York Guides: The Everything Guide to Brighton Beach |journal=New York |url=http://nymag.com/guides/everything/brighton-beach |access-date=November 12, 2015 |quote=Subtitle: Inside the land of pelmeni, matryoshkas, tracksuits, and of course, vodka. |archive-date=October 27, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191027214822/http://nymag.com/guides/everything/brighton-beach/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2006, [[Alec Brook-Krasny]] was elected for the 46th District of the [[New York State Assembly]], which includes Brighton Beach, becoming the country's first elected [[Soviet Union|Soviet]]-born politician.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter = The Dual Roles of Brighton Beach: A Local and Global Community|last = Conn|first = Phyllis|publisher = Lexington Books|year = 2012|isbn = 978-0-7391-6670-3|location = Lanham, MD|page = 352|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=g_BP-LiDDX0C&q=alec+brook-krasny+first+soviet&pg=PA352|title = The World in Brooklyn: Gentrification, Immigration, and Ethnic Politics in a Global City|editor-last = DeSena|editor-first = Judith}}</ref>

=== Demographics ===
{{See also|Demographics of Brooklyn}}
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of Brighton Beach was 35,547, an increase of 303 (0.9%) from the 35,244 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{convert|393.32|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|90.4|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre – New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610175331/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division – [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Retrieved June 16, 2016.</ref> The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 69.7% (24,774) [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 1.0% (352) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.2% (61) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 12.9% (4,580) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.0% (10) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 0.4% (139) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 1.2% (442) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 14.6% (5,189) of the population.<ref name="PLP3A">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin – New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610170733/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf |date=June 10, 2016 }}, Population Division – [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. Retrieved June 14, 2016.</ref>

In 1983, Brighton Beach consisted mostly of older, middle-class Jews; 27% of Brighton Beach was of age 62 or older, compared to the national average 13.9% at the time.<ref name="Dolan" /> Since the 1990s, however, the neighborhood's ethnic demographics have been changing, with a large influx of [[Central Asia]]n immigrants—namely [[Uzbeks]].<ref name="jewish daily forward 201209" /> In subsequent years, the proportion of whites leveled out, the proportion of blacks decreased significantly, and the proportion of Asians increased to 14% as of 2014.<ref name="censusreporter.org">{{Cite news|url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604018-nycbrooklyn-community-district-13brighton-beach--coney-island-puma-ny/|title=Census profile: NYC-Brooklyn Community District 13—Brighton Beach & Coney Island PUMA, NY|newspaper=Census Reporter|access-date=December 11, 2016|archive-date=December 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220123717/https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604018-nycbrooklyn-community-district-13brighton-beach--coney-island-puma-ny/|url-status=dead}}</ref> {{As of|2010}}, increasing numbers of Muslim [[Central Asians]] were moving into Brighton Beach, and based on the historic Soviet influence over these areas, these immigrants also speak Russian.<ref name="jewish daily forward 201209" /><ref>[http://pics.city-data.com/nraces/40751.jpg] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150326035941/http://pics.city-data.com/nraces/40751.jpg|date=March 26, 2015}}</ref>

According to the United States Census report of 2010, Brighton Beach and Coney Island, combined, had 111,063 residents as of 2009.<ref name="rpt8-2012">{{cite book |author1=DiNapoli, Thomas P. |author2=Bleiwas, Kenneth B. |year=2011 |title=Economic Snapshot of Coney Island and Brighton Beach [Report 8-2012, July 2011] |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Office of the State Comptroller, New York City Public Information Office |url=http://www.osc.state.ny.us/osdc/rpt8-2012.pdf |access-date=November 12, 2015 |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924062103/http://www.osc.state.ny.us/osdc/rpt8-2012.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> In that year, the median age of the combined Brighton Beach and Coney Island area was 47.9 years, substantially higher than the median age in Brooklyn of 34.2 and in [[New York City]] as a whole at 36.0.<ref name="rpt8-2012" /> As DiNapoli and Bleiwas note in a city report, "the number of residents aged 65 years and older in [this area] rose by 4.1 percent, so that senior citizens accounted for more than one-quarter of the area's population" at that date.<ref name="rpt8-2012" /> According to the census, the population density in Brighton Beach, per se (52,109 people per square mile), was almost twice the average population density of New York City (27,012 people per square mile), though the average household size was 2.1 people, lower than the city average of 2.6 people. The average income of households in the area was $36,574, while the average income in the whole city was $55,217, according to the 2010 census. In Brighton Beach, 21% of the population lives below the [[poverty line]],<ref name="censusreporter.org" /> compared to only 15.4% citywide.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://talkpoverty.org/state-year-report/new-york-2016-report/|title=New York Report – 2016 – Talk Poverty|newspaper=Talk Poverty|language=en-US|access-date=December 11, 2016|archive-date=December 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220102940/https://talkpoverty.org/state-year-report/new-york-2016-report/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Most of the population of Brighton Beach are immigrants. Less than a quarter (23.3%) of Brighton Beach residents were born in the United States, and nearly three-quarters were born abroad (72.9%). Because of this, English language proficiency in Brighton Beach is lower than the city average. More than a third (36.1%) of the population of Brighton Beach does not speak or understand English, while citywide, only one in fourteen people (7.2%) cannot speak or understand English.<ref name="rpt8-2012" />

The [[New York City Department of City Planning]] showed that in the 2020 census data that there were between 20,000 and 29,000 White residents and between 5,000 and 9,999 Asian residents, meanwhile each the Hispanic and Black populations were each less than 5000 residents.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/planning-level/nyc-population/census2020/dcp_2020-census-briefing-booklet-1.pdf|title=Key Population & Housing Characteristics; 2020 Census Results for New York City|publisher=[[New York City Department of City Planning]]|date=August 2021|access-date=November 7, 2021|pages=21, 25, 29, 33|archive-date=September 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210925151633/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/planning-level/nyc-population/census2020/dcp_2020-census-briefing-booklet-1.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Map: Race and ethnicity across the US | publisher=CNN | date=August 14, 2021 | url=https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2021/us/census-race-ethnicity-map/ | access-date=November 7, 2021 | archive-date=October 4, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211004102038/https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2021/us/census-race-ethnicity-map/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

== Police and crime ==
Brighton Beach is patrolled by the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]]'s 60th Precinct, located at 2950 West Eighth Street.<ref name="NYPD 60th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/60th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 60th Precinct|website=nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016|archive-date=June 7, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170607064341/http://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/60th-precinct.page|url-status=live}}</ref> The 60th Precinct ranked 34th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010. Between 1993 and 2010, major crimes decreased by 72%, including a 76% decrease in robberies, 71% decrease in felony assaults, and 67% decrease in shootings.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/coney-island/|title=Coney Island – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180723034345/https://www.dnainfo.com/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/coney-island/|archive-date=July 23, 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> The 60th Precinct has a substantially lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 77.5% between 1990 and 2022. The precinct reported five murders, 16 rapes, 179 robberies, 373 felony assaults, 159 burglaries, 527 grand larcenies, and 121 grand larcenies auto in 2022.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-060pct.pdf|title=60th Precinct CompStat Report|website=nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=July 22, 2018|archive-date=July 23, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180723034252/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-060pct.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

Brighton Beach is considered a hot spot for the [[Russian Mafia|Russian Bratva]],<ref>{{cite journal |year=1994 |journal=[[The New York Times]] |author=Raab, Selwyn |title=Influx of Russian Gangsters Troubles F.B.I. in Brooklyn |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/08/23/nyregion/influx-of-russian-gangsters-troubles-fbi-in-brooklyn.html |access-date=November 11, 2015 |archive-date=October 21, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171021233244/http://www.nytimes.com/1994/08/23/nyregion/influx-of-russian-gangsters-troubles-fbi-in-brooklyn.html |url-status=live }}</ref> though public perception has been that organized crime "has largely gone away."<ref>{{cite news |year=2008 |publisher=CBS News |title=Undercover Look Inside The Russian Mob |author=Keteyian, Armen |url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/undercover-look-inside-the-russian-mob/ |access-date=November 11, 2015 |archive-date=November 12, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151112201358/http://www.cbsnews.com/news/undercover-look-inside-the-russian-mob/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 1970s, the most notorious leg of the mafia was the [[Potato Bag Gang]],<ref>{{cite book |author1=Orleck, Annelise  |author2=Cooke, Elizabeth |title=The Soviet Jewish Americans |year=1999 |publisher=Greenwood Publishing |location=Westport, CT, USA |isbn=978-0-313-30074-5 |page=116 |url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=1584651385}}</ref> which served as a robbery gang for larger Russian crime syndicates in New York City. [[Marat Balagula]] was a crime boss from Brighton Beach who denies having any connection to the [[American Mafia]] or the Russian-speaking Mafia.{{citation needed|date=November 2015}} The major Russian criminal element in Brighton Beach was the international Russian mafia group, known as [[vor v zakone]] or "vory," and the first vory crime boss in Brighton Beach was [[Evsei Agron]], who controlled the area's crime during the 1970s and 1980s until his death in 1985.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.themoscowtimes.com/news/article/family-business-the-russian-mob-in-newyork/219074.html |title=Archived Document |access-date=November 30, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117040625/http://www.themoscowtimes.com/news/article/family-business-the-russian-mob-in-newyork/219074.html |archive-date=November 17, 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref> After the [[fall of the Soviet Union]] in the 1990s, many ethnic Russian criminals illegally entered the United States, coming especially to Brighton Beach.{{citation needed|date=November 2015}} The infamous vor [[Vyacheslav Ivankov]], who dominated the Brighton Beach underworld until his arrest in 1995, arrived during this wave.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/06/09/nyregion/reputed-russian-crime-chief-arrested.html |title=Reputed Russian crime chief arrested |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 9, 1995 |access-date=November 11, 2015 |last1=Raab |first1=Selwyn |archive-date=November 12, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151112201358/http://www.nytimes.com/1995/06/09/nyregion/reputed-russian-crime-chief-arrested.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Library ===
The [[Brooklyn Public Library]]'s Brighton Beach branch is located at 16 Brighton First Road, near Brighton Beach Avenue. The branch contains a large collection of media in Russian. The branch opened in December 1949, but due to high patronage, moved to its current location in 1964. The branch was renovated in the early 1990s.<ref>{{cite web | title=History | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=November 7, 2016 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/brighton-beach/history | access-date=February 23, 2019 | archive-date=February 24, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190224062628/https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/brighton-beach/history | url-status=live }}</ref>
